docs.title: spectracles
docs.text:
Continuous field models for integral field spectroscopy and beyond.

Spectracles fits models to IFU data where line or spectrum properties (line flux or velocity, continuum, ...) vary continuously across the sky. These are modelled as fields, so they are defined at every sky position spanned by the data, not just at the spaxels.

More generally, spectracles is a JAX library for statistical models with latent fields, built for large problems. Models are modular Equinox modules, and work with most JAX inference tools: MGVI and geoVI through NIFTy.re, NUTS through BlackJAX or NumPyro, or a best fit with optax.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install spectracles            # or: uv add spectracles
pip install "spectracles[nifty]"   # to use MGVI and geoVI
pip install blackjax               # to use NUTS

For SDSS-V LVM data, lvm_tools reads the DRP output (lazily, with dask) and gives you the data ready for spectracles: pip install "lvm-tools[spectracles]".

To run on a GPU, build jax-finufft from source as its README describes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A positive-valued field, observed with noise at 300 scattered points and fitted with NUTS:

import blackjax
import equinox as eqx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax import random

from spectracles import FourierGP, Matern32, Parameter, SpatialDataGeneric, build_model
from spectracles.inference import GaussianLikelihood, LatentSpace, Posterior
from spectracles.priors import LogNormal

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)


class LineMap(eqx.Module):
    log_flux: FourierGP

    def __call__(self, data):
        return jnp.exp(self.log_flux(data))


kernel = Matern32(
    length_scale=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(0.5, 0.2)),
    variance=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(1.0, 0.5)),
)
model = build_model(LineMap, FourierGP(kernel, n_modes=(15, 15)))
latent = LatentSpace(model)  # the parameters to fit

# Fake data from a random draw of the model
xy = random.uniform(random.PRNGKey(0), (2, 300), minval=-3.0, maxval=3.0)
spaxels = SpatialDataGeneric(x=xy[0], y=xy[1], idx=jnp.arange(300))
truth = latent.sample_prior_latent(random.PRNGKey(1))
flux = latent.to_model(truth)(spaxels) + 0.05 * random.normal(random.PRNGKey(2), (300,))
ivar = jnp.full(300, 0.05**-2)

posterior = Posterior(latent, lambda m: m(spaxels), GaussianLikelihood(flux, ivar))

# Sample with NUTS
n_steps = 300  # fast in tests: 10
warmup = blackjax.window_adaptation(blackjax.nuts, posterior.log_density)
(state, params), _ = warmup.run(random.PRNGKey(3), latent.zeros(), num_steps=n_steps)
nuts = blackjax.nuts(posterior.log_density, **params)


def step(state, key):
    state, _ = nuts.step(key, state)
    return state, state.position


_, samples = jax.lax.scan(step, state, random.split(random.PRNGKey(4), n_steps))

posterior.summary(samples, true_latents=truth)  # fitted parameters vs the truth
maps = posterior.draws(samples, to="model")(spaxels)  # the model for every sample
mean_map, std_map = maps.mean(), maps.std()

docs.title: Stability
docs.text:
From 1.0.0, spectracles follows semantic versioning: anything in spectracles, spectracles.priors, spectracles.inference or spectracles.nifty only changes in a major release, after a deprecation warning. Two parts are outside this promise:

Experimental: spectracles.lvm_models

The LVM-specific models are being ported to priors and the latent space one at a time.

Changing: OptimiserFrame and schedules

These will move onto the same posterior as the rest of spectracles. See the roadmap.

docs.title: Citation
docs.text: If you use spectracles, please cite Hilder et al. (2026), ApJ 997, 339. The README has the BibTeX entry and the other software to cite.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to spectracles are documented in this file.

The format follows Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Priors on parameters (spectracles.priors: StdNormal, Normal, LogNormal, Laplace, Uniform). Give one with Parameter(prior=...), or set them afterwards by glob with model.with_priors({...}); get_priors() lists them and model summaries have a Prior column. FourierGP coefficients have a standard-normal prior by default.
  • A latent space, likelihoods and a posterior (spectracles.inference: LatentSpace, Likelihood, GaussianLikelihood, Posterior). Every free parameter gets a standard-normal latent, so one model gives the same posterior, in the same coordinates, to MGVI/geoVI (NIFTy.re), NUTS (BlackJAX) and MAP (optax). GaussianLikelihood drops masked, non-finite and zero-weight data points.
  • spectracles.nifty: to_nifty(posterior) and stages(...) for staged variational inference with NIFTy.re. NIFTy is an optional extra: pip install "spectracles[nifty]".
  • Results from any backend's samples: Posterior.summary (with optional true values), draws (returning Draws of parameter values, or ModelDraws with to="model" to evaluate any part of the model at every sample), map_samples, to_model and to_params. Draws summaries reduce over the sample axes only (axis= picks some; reduce(fn) takes any statistic).
  • Posterior.fix and LatentSpace.fix: hold chosen parameters at given values for a whole fit.
  • ShareModule.for_evaluation(): an evaluable copy of a model, with shared values filled in.
  • ShareModule.set accepts a dict from path to value; build_model accepts an instance as well as a class.
  • Physical units: Domain(centre, extent) (or Domain.from_points(x, y)) describes the region the data cover, in the data's own units. FourierGP and FourierBasis take domain=, padding= (0.15 of the extent on each side by default) and nufft_tol=. With a domain, length scales are in the coordinates' units. Positions outside the periodic box raise an error.
  • Domain.grid((n, m), padding=0.0): a regular grid of points over the domain (or over a GP's whole box with padding=gp.padding), e.g. to map a field after fitting.
  • FourierGP(kernel, domain=...) chooses its own modes and padding for a tolerance (tol=1e-3 by default) over the length-scale prior's 1% to 99% quantiles (or length_scale=, or quantiles=). The choice is recorded in gp.design. n_modes= and padding= can still be given by hand.
  • spectracles.discretisation: discretisation_error (the truncation and aliasing errors of a FourierGP, or what they would be with other settings; an array of length scales gives a curve), required_modes, required_padding, realised_covariance, report (every FourierGP in a model, latent space or posterior, optionally across samples) and plot_discretisation.
  • Kernels: spectral_density and covariance, the continuous forms of the built-in kernels.
  • Fields: FourierGP(..., mean=Parameter(...)) adds a constant, and link="identity" | "exp" | "softplus" (with lower=) transforms the field, e.g. for a positive line flux. With a mean, the GP's own k = 0 mode is dropped and the mean alone sets the field's average over the box.
  • FieldFromRatio (a base field times 10 to the power of a log-ratio field) and FieldPlusScatter (a field plus independent scatter), exported from spectracles and built on mean= and link=. The experimental lvm_models keeps its own versions.
  • Clear errors where mistakes are common: wrong dims, n_modes that aren't two odd integers, a Prior passed positionally, wrong-sized per-spaxel, per-IFU or per-tile values (previously clamped silently), and a model passed to Posterior as forward.
  • Documentation: Building models, Priors and inference, How it works, Geometry and discretisation and LVM data guides; a worked inference example; a roadmap; this changelog and a contributing guide. The code on the guide pages is run by the tests.
  • Python 3.13 and 3.14 are tested in CI and listed in the package classifiers.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• FourierGP takes the kernel first: FourierGP(kernel, n_modes=..., ...). The old FourierGP(n_modes, kernel) still works, with a DeprecationWarning.
  • nufft_tol= on FourierGP and FourierBasis replaces the module-level FINUFFT_KWDS (the default accuracy, 1e-10, is unchanged).
  • A parameter with a prior and no initial value starts at the prior's median (it used to start at 0, possibly outside the prior's support).
  • SpatialData is a base class that SpatialDataGeneric and SpatialDataLVM subclass, so you can define your own spatial data classes. It used to be a type alias.
  • spectracles.lvm_models is marked experimental: it is not covered by the API stability promise and is not type-checked.
  • MultiFourierGP raises NotImplementedError until 1.1. Use one FourierGP per field.
  • A Parameter inside a list, tuple or dict raises a clear TypeError (support is planned for 1.1).
  • Models saved with save_model by earlier versions don't load correctly (models have new fields).
  • Summary tables wrap long parameter paths instead of truncating them.
  • The package passes pyright with no errors (excluding lvm_models).

docs.title: Deprecated
docs.text:

  • ShareModule.get_locked_model(): use for_evaluation(). It still works and warns.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Contributions to spectracles are welcome, whether a bug report, a fix, a new model component or a clearer page in these docs. This page describes how to set up a copy to work on and what a pull request needs.

docs.title: Setting up
docs.text:
spectracles uses uv to manage its environment. Clone the repository and install it with its development dependencies:

git clone https://github.com/TomHilder/spectracles.git
cd spectracles
uv sync

uv sync builds jax-finufft from source, from its git repository, so you need FFTW installed first (for example brew install fftw on macOS, or libfftw3-dev on Debian and Ubuntu). The development dependencies include NIFTy.re, BlackJAX and astropy, so the whole test suite can run.

Run any command in the environment with uv run, e.g. uv run python my_script.py.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
uv run pytest

runs everything. To run one file, one class or one test:

uv run pytest tests/test_spatial.py
uv run pytest tests/test_spatial.py::TestFourierGP
uv run pytest tests/test_spatial.py::TestFourierGP::test_realised_covariance

Add -x to stop at the first failure, or -k word to run only tests whose names contain word. Tests run in float64. New functionality should come with tests.

docs.title: Linting and formatting
docs.text:
The code is linted and formatted with Ruff, with a line length of 99:

uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format .

uv run ruff check --fix . fixes what it safely can. CI runs ruff check . and ruff format --check ., so run both before pushing.

docs.title: Type checking
docs.text:
The package is checked with pyright, which isn't in the development dependencies; install it however you like (for example pipx install pyright). Then

pyright src/spectracles

should report no errors. pyproject.toml points pyright at the project's .venv and excludes spectracles.lvm_models, which is experimental and not type-checked.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is Markdown in docs/, built with MkDocs Material, and the API reference is generated from docstrings by mkdocstrings. Preview it with live reload:

uv run --with mkdocs-material --with "mkdocstrings[python]" mkdocs serve

and open the address it prints. To check that it builds without warnings, as CI does:

uv run --with mkdocs-material --with "mkdocstrings[python]" mkdocs build --strict

New pages go in the nav section of mkdocs.yml. CI builds the docs on every pull request and deploys them when a version is tagged.

docs.title: Code on the docs pages is tested
docs.text:
tests/test_docs.py runs the ```python blocks of the guide and example pages, in order, as one script per page, so the examples can't go stale. Pages are listed in its PAGES dict with any optional packages they need. If you add a guide page with code, add it there too.

  • A block whose first line is # sketch is illustrative only and is skipped.
  • A line like n_draws = 600 # fast in tests: 20 runs with the faster value in the tests, while readers see the real one.

Run just these tests with uv run pytest tests/test_docs.py.

docs.title: Docstrings
docs.text: Docstrings use Google style (Args:, Returns:, Raises: sections), which the API reference renders. Describe what the code does and how to use it. Leave out its history (what it used to do, why it changed, how it was tested): that belongs in commit messages and the changelog.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
1. Create a branch from main (on a fork, if you don't have write access).
  2. Make your changes, with tests and docs as needed.
  3. Add an entry to the changelog under Unreleased, in the right group (Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed or Fixed). Say plainly if the change affects results or breaks existing code.
  4. Open a pull request against main.

CI must pass: the lint job (ruff check and ruff format --check), the tests on Python 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14, and the strict docs build.

docs.title: Reporting issues
docs.text: Report bugs and request features through GitHub Issues. For a bug, include your Python, JAX and spectracles versions, a small example that shows the problem, and the full error message.

docs.title: Geometry and discretisation
docs.text:
A FourierGP represents a field by Fourier modes on a box. This page explains how that box relates to your data, how accurate the field is, and how spectracles chooses the number of modes for you. To build fields in the first place, see Building models.

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax import random

from spectracles import Domain, FourierGP, Matern32, Parameter, SpatialDataGeneric
from spectracles.priors import LogNormal

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
spectracles doesn't know about arcseconds or parsecs. Positions can be in any units, and a field's length scale is in the same units. For LVM data, positions in arcseconds from the centre of the field are a good choice: length-scale priors are then in arcseconds too.

A Domain is the square region your data cover, in those units:

xy = random.uniform(random.PRNGKey(0), (2, 500), minval=-600.0, maxval=600.0)
spaxels = SpatialDataGeneric(x=xy[0], y=xy[1], idx=jnp.arange(500))

domain = Domain.from_points(spaxels.x, spaxels.y)
print(domain)

Domain(centre=(0.9374042496963852, 0.3712791182837236), extent=1198.303547276262)

Domain(centre=(x, y), extent=side) sets it directly. Several fields can share one domain.

docs.title: Two kinds of error
docs.text:
The field lives on a periodic box: the domain plus a margin of padding on each side. Its covariance then differs from the kernel's in two ways:

  • Truncation. The modes stop at a highest frequency, so structure finer than the spacing of the mode grid is missing. This matters for short length scales, and more modes fix it.
  • Aliasing. The box wraps around, so each point is also correlated with copies of the others one box-width away. This matters for long length scales, and more padding fixes it.

Both are measured relative to the field's variance. The truncation error is an average over pairs of points spread across the domain; the aliasing error is the worst pair, since it couples opposite edges of the data.

docs.title: Modes chosen for you
docs.text:
Given a domain, a FourierGP chooses its own padding and modes, so that both errors are below a tolerance (0.1% by default) for every length scale between its prior's 1% and 99% quantiles:

kernel = Matern32(
    length_scale=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(40.0, 12.0)),
    variance=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(1.0, 0.5)),
)
field = FourierGP(kernel, domain=domain)
print(field.n_modes, field.padding)
print(field.design)  # (tol, shortest, longest length scale) it was chosen for

(163, 163) 0.3
(0.001, 19.4..., 75.8...)

The padding is set by the longest length scale: keeping aliasing below 0.1% needs a gap of about ten length scales between the data and their periodic copies. The modes are set by the shortest. A wide prior costs both. You can change what the choice is made for:

FourierGP(kernel, domain=domain, tol=1e-2)  # 1% instead of 0.1%
FourierGP(kernel, domain=domain, length_scale=(20.0, 100.0))  # your own range
FourierGP(kernel, domain=domain, quantiles=(0.05, 0.95))  # a narrower part of the prior

or set the modes and padding yourself:

by_hand = FourierGP(kernel, domain=domain, n_modes=(101, 101), padding=0.2)

Choosing takes a few seconds per field, once, when the model is built.

docs.title: What error would I get?
docs.text:
discretisation_error gives both errors for a field as it is, or as it would be with a different length scale, number of modes or padding:

from spectracles.discretisation import discretisation_error

print(discretisation_error(by_hand))
print(discretisation_error(by_hand, length_scale=15.0).truncation)  # if ℓ were 15″
print(discretisation_error(by_hand, n_modes=51).truncation)  # with fewer modes
print(discretisation_error(by_hand, padding=0.05).aliasing)  # with less padding

It works for a kernel before you build any field, too:

e = discretisation_error(kernel, domain=domain, n_modes=101, padding=0.2, length_scale=30.0)

An array of length scales gives the errors along it, e.g. for a plot:

import numpy as np

curve = discretisation_error(by_hand, length_scale=np.geomspace(5.0, 300.0, 30))
curve.truncation, curve.aliasing  # arrays, one value per length scale

required_modes and required_padding answer the opposite question: what does a given accuracy need?

from spectracles.discretisation import required_modes, required_padding

required_modes(kernel, domain, length_scale=20.0, padding=0.2, tol=1e-3)  # modes per side
required_padding(kernel, domain, length_scale=80.0, tol=1e-3)  # fraction of the extent

docs.title: Checking a fit
docs.text:
The length scales a fit finds can fall outside the range a field was built for. report checks every field in a model at each sample, at the shortest length scale found (for truncation) and the longest (for aliasing):

import equinox as eqx

from spectracles import build_model
from spectracles.discretisation import report
from spectracles.inference import LatentSpace


class Map(eqx.Module):
    flux: FourierGP

    def __call__(self, data):
        return self.flux(data)


latent = LatentSpace(build_model(Map, flux=field))
samples = latent.sample_prior_latent(random.PRNGKey(1), n=100)  # stand-in for posterior samples
rows = report(latent, samples)

It prints a table with one row per field, and warns if any is above its tolerance. Here it does: 100 draws from the prior reach beyond its 1%–99% range, which the field was built for. After a real fit, a warning means the posterior found length scales the field can't represent accurately; rebuild it for the range found (length_scale=(shortest, longest)). It also takes a Posterior, or a model on its own to check its current values. plot_discretisation shows one field's errors against the length scale, with the length scales found as ticks:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from spectracles.discretisation import plot_discretisation

found = latent.to_params(samples)["flux.kernel.length_scale"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
plot_discretisation(field, length_scales=found, ax=ax)
fig.savefig("discretisation.png")

The shaded range is what the field was built for. Truncation (left) is under the tolerance at its short end, and aliasing (right) at its long end.

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
With Δ the spacing of the mode grid (the box side divided by the number of modes) and the gap the distance between the data's far edge and its periodic copy (twice the padding times the extent), the errors depend only on ℓ/Δ and gap/ℓ:

Kernel 1%: ℓ_min/Δ 1%: gap/ℓ_max 0.1%: ℓ_min/Δ 0.1%: gap/ℓ_max Matern12 ≥ 3.0 ≥ 5 ≥ 9.6 ≥ 7 Matern32 ≥ 0.88 ≥ 7 ≥ 1.64 ≥ 10 Matern52 ≥ 0.58 ≥ 8 ≥ 0.90 ≥ 11 SquaredExponential ≥ 0.92 ≥ 3 ≥ 1.13 ≥ 4

Length scales here are spectracles' own: a Matérn kernel's is the textbook one divided by √(2ν).

docs.title: Without a domain
docs.text: A FourierGP without a domain works as in earlier versions: positions must already lie in [−π, π], the length scale is in those units, there is no padding, and n_modes must be given. The diagnostic still works on it.

docs.title: Kernels of your own
docs.text: Choosing modes, and the diagnostic, need the kernel's continuous form: its spectral density and covariance (Kernel.spectral_density and Kernel.covariance). The built-in kernels have both. For a kernel without them, give n_modes and padding yourself.

docs.title: Priors and inference
docs.text:
To fit a spectracles model with Bayesian inference, you put a prior on each parameter you want to fit, describe the noise in your data with a likelihood, and hand the result to a fitting method. The same model works with:

  • MGVI and geoVI, through NIFTy.re;
  • NUTS, through BlackJAX;
  • a best fit (MAP), through optax.

Switching method changes how the fit is done, not the problem being solved.

This page is the practical guide. How it works explains the design in more depth. To build the model in the first place, see Building models.

docs.title: Priors, likelihoods and posteriors in one minute
docs.text:
When you fit a model to an IFU cube, you are estimating maps (a line flux, a velocity field) together with a few global numbers, such as how quickly those maps vary.

  • A prior says which values are plausible before you look at the data. For example, "the correlation length is around 0.5, give or take 0.2", or "the per-spaxel offsets are small".
  • The likelihood says how probable the observed spectra are for given parameter values. For Gaussian noise of known variance, it is the familiar χ².
  • The posterior combines the two: what is plausible after seeing the data. A best fit is its peak. Samples from it give uncertainties on every map and every quantity you derive from them.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
pip install "spectracles[nifty]"   # for MGVI and geoVI
pip install blackjax               # for NUTS

Inference should be done in double precision:

import jax

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

docs.title: A running example
docs.text:
A line-flux map, made of a positive Gaussian-process field plus a small offset per spaxel, observed at 300 spaxels:

import equinox as eqx
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax import random

from spectracles import (
    FourierGP,
    Matern32,
    Parameter,
    PerSpaxel,
    SpatialDataGeneric,
    build_model,
)
from spectracles.priors import Laplace, LogNormal


class LineMap(eqx.Module):
    """A line-flux map: a log-normal GP field plus a small per-spaxel offset."""

    log_flux: FourierGP
    offset: PerSpaxel

    def __call__(self, data):
        return jnp.exp(self.log_flux(data)) + self.offset(data)


N_SPAXELS = 300
xy = random.uniform(random.PRNGKey(0), (2, N_SPAXELS), minval=-3.0, maxval=3.0)
spaxels = SpatialDataGeneric(x=xy[0], y=xy[1], idx=jnp.arange(N_SPAXELS))

docs.title: Declaring priors
docs.text:
Give a Parameter its prior when you create it:

kernel = Matern32(
    length_scale=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(0.5, 0.2)),
    variance=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(1.0, 0.5)),
)
model = build_model(
    LineMap,
    log_flux=FourierGP(kernel, n_modes=(21, 21)),
    offset=PerSpaxel(N_SPAXELS),
)

The priors are in spectracles.priors:

Prior Arguments Use it for StdNormal() none GP coefficients (the default for them) Normal(mean, std) mean and standard deviation offsets, calibration terms LogNormal(mean, std) mean and standard deviation of the value itself positive quantities: length scales, variances, amplitudes Laplace(alpha) scale (centred on 0) corrections that are mostly near zero Uniform(low, high) bounds a bounded quantity with no preferred value

A parameter with a prior starts at the prior's median, unless you give it a starting value: Parameter(0.7, prior=...).

A prior's arguments are single numbers, and apply to every element of the parameter (e.g. every spaxel of a PerSpaxel).

FourierGP gives its coefficients a StdNormal prior automatically, since the kernel already sets their scale. If you pass in your own coefficients parameter, give it prior=StdNormal() yourself.

You can also set priors after building the model, by path or by glob pattern (* matches one part of a path, ** any number of parts):

model = model.with_priors({"offset.spaxel_values": Laplace(0.02)})

A value of "fixed" fixes the matching parameters instead, e.g. model.with_priors({"**.variance": "fixed"}). with_priors returns a new model and leaves the old one unchanged.

docs.title: Free, fixed and Known
docs.text:
Every number in a model that isn't data is one of three kinds.

A free Parameter, such as Parameter(prior=LogNormal(0.5, 0.2)), is something you want to learn from the data. It needs a prior.

A fixed Parameter, such as Parameter(0.5, fixed=True), is something you've chosen not to fit, for now. It keeps its value, but it is still a parameter: it shows up in summaries, model.set can change it, and it can be freed again. with_priors({...: "fixed"}), posterior.fix and staged fits all fix parameters.

Known(value) is a constant, such as a rest wavelength or the instrument's line-spread width. It can never be fitted. Summaries leave it out (pass show_knowns=True to include it), and model.set won't change it unless you pass allow_set_knowns=True.

If you might ever want to fit it, make it a Parameter. If it's a fact about the world or the instrument, make it Known. While fitting, fixed parameters and Known values behave the same way.

Declared as Fitted? Parameter(prior=P) or Parameter(value, prior=P) yes Parameter(value, fixed=True) no; it keeps its value Known(value) no; it's a constant Parameter(value), free, no prior error: give it a prior, or fix it ConstrainedParameter(...), free error: use a Parameter with a prior instead; the prior sets the range (e.g. LogNormal for positive values)

A parameter shared between two parts of the model (say, one velocity field used by two lines) is fitted once, with one prior. Two separate parameters that happen to have the same prior are fitted independently.

docs.title: The posterior
docs.text:
A Posterior brings together three things:

  • the model's free parameters and their priors, collected by LatentSpace;
  • a forward model: a function that turns the model into a prediction with the same shape as your data;
  • a likelihood for the data.

Here we simulate data from a random draw of the model, with 10 spaxels set to NaN:

import numpy as np

from spectracles.inference import GaussianLikelihood, LatentSpace, Posterior

latent = LatentSpace(model)

truth = latent.sample_prior_latent(random.PRNGKey(2))
noise = 0.05
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
flux = np.asarray(latent.to_model(truth)(spaxels)) + noise * rng.standard_normal(N_SPAXELS)
ivar = np.full(N_SPAXELS, noise**-2)
flux[:10] = np.nan  # e.g. bad fibres


def forward(m):
    return m(spaxels)


posterior = Posterior(latent, forward, GaussianLikelihood(flux, ivar))
print(posterior)

Posterior(LatentSpace(4 parameters, 743 latent dimensions), GaussianLikelihood on 290 data points)

For spectra, the forward model is usually the model evaluated at every wavelength: lambda m: jax.vmap(m, in_axes=(0, None))(wavelengths, spatial_data).

GaussianLikelihood(data, ivar, mask) skips data points that are masked, NaN, or have an inverse variance of zero, so bad pixels in real data are safe.

For other noise models, write your own likelihood by subclassing spectracles.inference.Likelihood (see its API reference). GaussianLikelihood is a short example of one.

docs.title: Fitting
docs.text: Every method works on the same function, posterior.log_density. It is plain JAX, so jit, grad and vmap all work on it.

docs.title: MGVI and geoVI (NIFTy.re)
docs.text:
to_nifty turns the posterior into something NIFTy can fit:

import nifty.re as jft

from spectracles.nifty import to_nifty

lh = to_nifty(posterior)
key_init, key_vi = random.split(random.PRNGKey(3))
samples, state = jft.optimize_kl(
    lh,
    jft.Vector(lh.init(key_init)),
    key=key_vi,
    n_total_iterations=4,
    n_samples=2,  # pairs of mirrored samples
    sample_mode="linear_resample",  # MGVI; "nonlinear_resample" for geoVI
    kl_kwargs={"minimize_kwargs": {"maxiter": 20}},
)

Real fits use more iterations and samples. NIFTy's documentation covers the settings.

docs.title: NUTS (BlackJAX)
docs.text:
posterior.log_density can be passed straight to BlackJAX. NIFTy isn't needed:

# sketch
import blackjax

warmup = blackjax.window_adaptation(blackjax.nuts, posterior.log_density)
(state, parameters), _ = warmup.run(key, latent.zeros(), num_steps=500)
nuts = blackjax.nuts(posterior.log_density, **parameters)
# ...then the usual BlackJAX sampling loop over nuts.step

The worked example runs this end to end.

docs.title: Best fit (MAP, with optax)
docs.text:
The best fit minimises -posterior.log_density:

import optax

optimiser = optax.adam(0.05)
ξ = latent.zeros()  # start from the priors' medians
opt_state = optimiser.init(ξ)


@jax.jit
def step(ξ, opt_state):
    loss, grad = jax.value_and_grad(lambda x: -posterior.log_density(x))(ξ)
    updates, opt_state = optimiser.update(grad, opt_state)
    return optax.apply_updates(ξ, updates), opt_state, loss


for _ in range(300):
    ξ, opt_state, loss = step(ξ, opt_state)
map_model = latent.to_model(ξ)

The fit works on rescaled versions of the parameters (ξ, see Under the hood), and latent.to_model turns the result back into a model.

docs.title: Fixing parameters for a whole fit
docs.text:
fix gives a new posterior with some parameters held at chosen values. It works with every method, and the original posterior is unchanged:

fixed = posterior.fix({"log_flux.kernel.length_scale": 0.5})
print(len(posterior.latent.paths), len(fixed.latent.paths))

4 3

A single number fills a parameter of any shape.

docs.title: Staged fits
docs.text:
With NIFTy, stages holds some parameters fixed for the first few iterations only. It uses the same words as the schedule builder (free_in, free_after, free_until, fixed_in), counting VI iterations:

from spectracles import fixed_in
from spectracles.nifty import stages

staging = stages(latent, {"offset.*": fixed_in(0, 1)}, n_iterations=4)
print(staging["constants"](0), staging["constants"](2))

('offset.spaxel_values',) ()

Pass it to NIFTy with jft.optimize_kl(..., **staging).

docs.title: Parameter values
docs.text:
posterior.draws(samples) gives the parameter values at every sample. Index it by path, and summarise over the samples:

params = posterior.draws(samples)
params.mean()  # {path: mean}
params["log_flux.kernel.length_scale"].std()

.values holds the samples themselves, e.g. for a corner plot.

docs.title: Maps
docs.text:
With to="model", you get the model at every sample. Call it like the model, and summarise the result:

models = posterior.draws(samples, to="model")
maps = models(spaxels)  # the whole model, at every sample
mean_map, std_map = maps.mean(), maps.std()
lower, upper = maps.quantile(0.16), maps.quantile(0.84)

Any part of the model works the same way, even parts that use shared parameters:

flux = models.log_flux(spaxels).mean()

maps.reduce(fn) applies any other statistic, e.g. maps.reduce(jnp.var).

docs.title: Anything else you compute from the model
docs.text:
For a quantity that isn't a single call, such as a ratio of two fields, give map_samples a function of the model:

ratio = posterior.map_samples(lambda m: m.log_flux(spaxels) - m.offset(spaxels), samples)
predictions = posterior.map_samples(posterior.forward, samples).mean()

docs.title: Several chains
docs.text:
NUTS chains stacked as (chain, draw, ...) are summarised over both axes. Give axis= to summarise over some of them, e.g. maps.mean(axis=1) for the mean of each chain.

Everything is held in memory. For very large fields, evaluate on fewer points or fewer samples at a time.

Which posterior mean?

For a nonlinear model, these give different answers:

  • the mean of each parameter: posterior.draws(samples).mean();
  • the model at the mean parameters: posterior.to_model(posterior.draws(samples).mean(), space="params");
  • the mean of a derived quantity, such as a map: maps.mean().

For maps and their uncertainties, use the last. Averaging the GP coefficients first gives a map smoother than any sample.

docs.title: With ArviZ
docs.text:
Parameter values keep the layout of the samples, (draw, ...) or (chain, draw, ...). That is what ArviZ expects:

import arviz as az


def for_arviz(values, chains=False):
    """{path: array} -> ArviZ variables, adding a chain axis if there isn't one.
    GP coefficients are left out: they are large and rarely wanted."""
    return {p: v if chains else v[None] for p, v in values.items() if "coefficients" not in p}


idata = az.from_dict(
    {
        "posterior": for_arviz(posterior.draws(samples).values),
        "prior": for_arviz(latent.sample_prior_params(random.PRNGKey(3), n=500)),
    }
)
print(az.summary(idata, var_names=["log_flux.kernel.length_scale"], kind="stats"))

                                mean    sd eti89_lb eti89_ub
log_flux.kernel.length_scale[0]  0.8  0.19     0.63     0.98

For chains run in parallel, pass chains=True.

Convergence diagnostics are for MCMC only

MGVI and geoVI samples are not Markov chains, so R-hat and effective sample sizes mean nothing for them. Use ArviZ's summaries and plots for VI samples, and its diagnostics only for NUTS.

docs.title: Checking your priors
docs.text:
Before fitting, it's worth checking that your priors give sensible maps. Draws from the prior come as a model, as parameter values, or as latents:

draw = latent.sample_prior_model(random.PRNGKey(1))
prior_map = draw(spaxels)  # a line-flux map drawn from the priors

ls = latent.sample_prior_params(random.PRNGKey(2), n=1000)["log_flux.kernel.length_scale"]
print(ls.shape, float(ls.mean()))  # 1000 prior draws of the length scale

Prior draws of parameter values can be summarised like posterior samples. Say that they are already parameter values with space="params":

prior_values = latent.sample_prior_params(random.PRNGKey(4), n=500)
prior_summary = posterior.summary(prior_values, space="params", print_table=False)

docs.title: Under the hood: the latent space
docs.text:
You rarely need this section, but it explains what the fitting methods actually see.

Each element of each free parameter is written as a standard-normal number, ξ, passed through its prior. For example, LogNormal(0.5, 0.2) turns ξ = 0 into its median and ξ = ±1 into roughly its ±1σ values. Every fitting method works with ξ, where all parameters are on the same scale. LatentSpace holds this mapping:

print(latent)
print(latent.paths)

LatentSpace(4 parameters, 743 latent dimensions)
['log_flux.coefficients', 'log_flux.kernel.length_scale', 'log_flux.kernel.variance', 'offset.spaxel_values']

ξ is a dict keyed by parameter path. The latent space converts it:

  • latent.to_params(ξ) gives the parameter values;
  • latent.to_model(ξ) gives a model with those values;
  • latent.from_model(model) goes back from a model to ξ, e.g. to start a fit from an earlier one.

Functions that take samples assume they are ξ, as fitting methods return them. For parameter values, pass space="params".

docs.title: Two ways to fit
docs.text: spectracles also has an older way to get a best fit: OptimiserFrame and schedules, with a loss you write yourself. It ignores priors. Use it for quick best fits with a custom loss, and the posterior for uncertainties. The two will be merged (see the roadmap).

docs.title: Current limitations
docs.text:
• Priors are independent. A prior can't depend on another parameter, except through the field hierarchy that FourierGP builds in.
  • Prior arguments are single numbers. There's a workaround for giving each element its own prior in How it works.
  • from_model is exact only for some priors (StdNormal, Normal, LogNormal). Others fall back to the prior median, with a warning.
  • Parameters in lists, tuples or dicts aren't supported yet (planned for 1.1), and MultiFourierGP is disabled until then. See Building models.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: The practical guide shows how to use priors, the latent space and the backends. This page explains the design behind them, and the points that matter when you rely on the results.

docs.title: One problem, in latent coordinates
docs.text:
Every free parameter θᵢ is written as a deterministic transform of standard-normal latents:

\[ \theta_i = T_i(\xi_i), \qquad \xi_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\ \text{(elementwise)}, \]

where Tᵢ is the transform of the parameter's prior. The posterior over the latents is then

\[ \log p(\xi \mid d) = \log L\big(d \mid F(\theta(\xi))\big) - \tfrac12 \lVert \xi \rVert^2 + \text{const}, \]

with F the forward model and L the likelihood. This one function is Posterior.log_density. Every backend works on it, in these coordinates.

Why standard-normal coordinates:

  • They are what MGVI and geoVI assume. NIFTy's methods are built around a standard-normal prior on the latents. Their metric is the likelihood's Fisher information plus the identity (see below).
  • They are good coordinates for NUTS and optimisers. Parameters with wildly different scales become order-one numbers. The GP hierarchy is non-centred (next section), which removes the "funnel" between a field and its hyperparameters that makes centred parametrisations hard to sample.
  • The prior needs no density. In ξ the prior is always −½|ξ|², so priors are only ever transforms. That's why each prior class implements a transform and (optionally) its inverse, and no log-density.
  • Every method sees the same problem. Results from MGVI, NUTS and MAP differ because the methods differ, not because they were handed different parametrisations of the model.

docs.title: Why no probabilistic programming language
docs.text:
The only hierarchy in these models is GP hyperparameters → field, and FourierGP already handles it internally. The field is

\[ f(x) = \sum_k \sqrt{P(k;\ell, s^2)}\; c_k\, e^{i k \cdot x}, \]

where the coefficients c are whitened: the power spectrum P scales them. The coefficients' prior is therefore N(0, 1) whatever the hyperparameters are, and each hyperparameter can have its own independent prior. This is the non-centred parametrisation, built into the model. Priors can stay as independent data on each parameter, with no graph of dependencies, which is why spectracles has Parameter(prior=...) rather than sample() statements.

docs.title: Transforms and conventions
docs.text:
Prior T(ξ) Inverse StdNormal() ξ ✓ Normal(m, s) m + s ξ ✓ LogNormal(mean, std) exp(μ + σ ξ), with σ² = log(1 + std²/mean²), μ = log(mean) − σ²/2 ✓ Laplace(α) the Laplace quantile function of Φ(ξ), computed from log Φ for accuracy in the tails — Uniform(a, b) a + (b − a) Φ(ξ) —
  • LogNormal is parametrised by the mean and standard deviation of the value itself, not of its logarithm. It is moment-matched, as in NIFTy.re.
  • spectracles implements these transforms itself, so the latent space and the log-density work without NIFTy installed. The tests check them against NIFTy's own priors to rtol 1e-14 when NIFTy is available.
  • Inverses are only used by LatentSpace.from_model, which maps existing values back to ξ (for example, to start a fit from an earlier one). Uniform's inverse is badly conditioned at the bounds (values there map to ξ = ±∞), and neither Uniform nor Laplace has one yet. from_model falls back to ξ = 0 for them, and for values outside a prior's support, with a warning naming the parameters.

docs.title: Shared parameters are one parameter
docs.text:
Sharing in spectracles is by object identity: one Parameter object used in several places. For inference that means:

  • one latent, keyed by the parent path;
  • one prior and one value. The value is written once and read everywhere;
  • gradients add up from every place the parameter is used.

Two separate Parameters that happen to have equal priors (even the same Prior object) are two independent parameters. This is why the prior is a static field on Parameter: if it were an array leaf, a Prior reused between parameters would look like shared arrays to ShareModule, and an optimiser would try to train its hyperparameters.

If parameters share only their value array (e.g. via eqx.tree_at) but carry different priors, validate_sharing reports it and LatentSpace refuses the model. One parameter can't have two priors.

docs.title: What each backend sees
docs.text:
Write J for the Jacobian of the forward model with respect to ξ, and N for the noise covariance (for GaussianLikelihood, diagonal with entries 1/ivar).

  • MAP (optax) maximises log_density.
  • NUTS (BlackJAX) samples exp(log_density).
  • MGVI and geoVI (NIFTy).
  • to_nifty gives NIFTy the forward model and the likelihood. NIFTy works with an energy E(ξ) = −log L(ξ) + ½|ξ|², without normalisation constants.
  • MGVI approximates the posterior around the current mean ξ̄ by a Gaussian whose precision is the metric M(ξ̄) = Jᵀ N⁻¹ J + 1.
  • geoVI additionally uses the metric's square root, Jᵀ N^{-1/2}, to curve the approximation.

The test suite checks that these are all the same object, without running any inference:

  • NIFTy's forward model and energy gradient match spectracles';
  • NIFTy's metric equals Jᵀ N⁻¹ J computed independently, and the square root composes to it;
  • NIFTy's own BlackJAX target and a BlackJAX NUTS state match log_density;
  • for a linear-Gaussian model, the Hessian of log_density equals the metric plus identity exactly, so MGVI's Gaussian and NUTS's target are literally the same distribution there.

All of this agrees to rtol 1e-14 on CPU.

docs.title: Masking without NaN gradients
docs.text: Real data have masked data points, whose values are often NaN. A likelihood written as jnp.where(mask, logpdf(data, pred), 0) gives the right value, but its gradient is NaN: where multiplies the unused branch's derivative by zero, and 0 × NaN = NaN. GaussianLikelihood removes masked data points when it is built (keeping the indices of the used data points), so masked values never enter a computation. It also drops data points with a non-finite value or an inverse variance ≤ 0.

docs.title: Staging
docs.text:
NIFTy has two separate per-iteration settings, and stages sets both:

  • constants: these latents are not updated by the KL minimisation;
  • point_estimates: no samples are drawn along these latents.

With constants alone, a "frozen" parameter keeps its mean but samples are still drawn along it, so it isn't really frozen. On a test problem, the sample spread of frozen hyperparameters was 0.03–0.8 in ξ with constants alone, and exactly 0 with both settings. A parameter that stages reports as not free is therefore in both lists, and fully frozen.

docs.title: Hyperparameters are the hard part
docs.text:
GP hyperparameters (length scale, variance) are weakly constrained by the data and strongly correlated with the field, so they are usually the hardest part of the posterior to explore:

  • MGVI and geoVI approximate the posterior locally (by a Gaussian, or a curved one for geoVI), built from a finite number of samples. Treat their hyperparameter estimates and uncertainties as approximate.
  • NUTS can mix slowly along these directions. Run long chains from several starting points and check convergence, e.g. with R-hat.

docs.title: MAP in latent space vs the old losses
docs.text:
The older losses in spectracles.lvm_models add FourierGP.prior_logpdf to the log-likelihood. prior_logpdf is the density of the scaled coefficients √P · c, which includes the Jacobian term −Σ log √P(k; ℓ, s²). That term depends on the hyperparameters. A MAP in ξ has no such term: its prior is just −½|ξ|².

MAP is not invariant to reparametrisation, so the two optima are different points whenever hyperparameters are free. Neither is wrong; they are different problems. Results from the old path and from the posterior should not be expected to agree exactly.

docs.title: Reproducibility of VI runs
docs.text:
For fixed inputs and keys, NIFTy's MGVI and geoVI are bit-for-bit reproducible. They are, however, sensitive to the last bit of the input.

On a 6-iteration test problem, changing the data by one unit in the last place moved the posterior mean by: - MGVI: about 0.06σ rms, up to about 0.8σ in places; - geoVI: about 0.07σ rms, up to about 1σ in places.

Here σ is the posterior standard deviation. The minimisers hit their iteration limits, so tiny differences take different paths. Two mathematically identical implementations of a model can therefore give visibly different VI results. Compare runs statistically (several seeds, or against NUTS), not bit for bit.

docs.title: Limitations and extension points
docs.text:
• Scalar hyperparameters only. Every element of a parameter gets the same prior. To give elements different priors, put a StdNormal on the parameter and build the value in the model from Known arrays:
# sketch
class PerTileOffset(eqx.Module):
    raw: Parameter  # prior=StdNormal()
    mean: Known  # per-tile prior means
    std: Known  # per-tile prior widths

    def __call__(self, data):
        return (self.mean.val + self.std.val * self.raw.val)[data.tile_idx]
  • No dependent priors beyond the GP hierarchy. A prior can't depend on another parameter.
  • Likelihoods: only GaussianLikelihood so far. A Student-t likelihood and a learned noise scaling are planned. They will map to NIFTy's StudentT and VariableCovarianceGaussian.
  • Two ways to fit. The optimiser path (OptimiserFrame, schedules) ignores priors. Unifying it with the latent space, so that optimisation also happens in ξ, is planned.

docs.title: LVM data with lvm_tools
docs.text:
lvm_tools reads SDSS-V Local Volume Mapper data reduction pipeline (DRP) files and prepares them for spectracles. It selects a wavelength window and a region of sky, drops bad fibres and pixels, scales the flux, and gives each spaxel's position in arcseconds from the centre of the field. Files are read lazily with dask, so only the window you ask for is loaded.

pip install "lvm-tools[spectracles]>=0.2"

This page fits an Hα map to LVM data, from DRP files to a map on the sky. The code needs your own data files, so it isn't run when the docs are built.

docs.title: Loading the data
docs.text:
Each DRP file (an lvmSFrame) is one exposure of one pointing. Load the ones you want and combine them:

# sketch
from pathlib import Path

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

from lvm_tools import DataConfig, FitDataBuilder, LVMTile, LVMTileCollection

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

files = sorted(Path("path/to/drp").glob("lvmSFrame-*.fits"))
tiles = LVMTileCollection.from_tiles([LVMTile.from_file(f) for f in files])

DataConfig says which part of the data to use. Here, a 20 Å window around Hα; the sky region defaults to everything in the files:

# sketch
config = DataConfig.from_tiles(tiles, λ_range=(6553.0, 6573.0))
data = FitDataBuilder(tiles, config).build()

print(config) shows every setting, including how bad data are handled and how the flux is scaled. The lvm_tools docs cover the options.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
data holds everything the fit needs:

Shape data.flux, data.i_var (wavelengths, spaxels) flux and inverse variance, scaled data.mask (wavelengths, spaxels) True where a pixel is good data.λ (wavelengths,) wavelengths in Å data.lsf_σ (wavelengths, spaxels) the line-spread function's width in Å data.sky_data the spaxel positions, as a SpatialDataLVM

data.sky_data is what a spectracles model is evaluated at. Its positions x and y are each spaxel's offset east and north of the field's centre (data.sky_centre), in arcseconds, on the tangent plane. It also carries each spaxel's tile, IFU and fibre, for the per-tile and per-IFU models in spectracles.model.spatial.

The flux and inverse variance are scaled consistently, so fitted fluxes are in the scaled units. config.normalise_F_scale and config.normalise_F_offset convert them back.

By default the flux is divided by its maximum. If there are bright stars in the field, the maximum is a star, and nebular lines end up small in the scaled units. DataConfig.from_tiles(..., normalise_F_strategy="98 only") scales by the 98th percentile instead.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
An Hα line whose flux, velocity and width are all fields, plus a constant continuum per spaxel. The width is a typical value times a positive field, so it can vary across the sky. The line-spread function is a Known value per spaxel, taken from the data and added to the line's width:

# sketch
import equinox as eqx

from spectracles import FourierGP, Known, Matern32, Parameter, PerSpaxel, build_model
from spectracles.priors import LogNormal, Normal

C_KMS = 299_792.458
HALPHA = 6562.8


class Halpha(eqx.Module):
    log_flux: FourierGP
    velocity: FourierGP
    log_width: FourierGP
    typical_width: Parameter
    lsf: Known
    continuum: PerSpaxel

    def __call__(self, λ, spaxels):
        centre = HALPHA * (1 + self.velocity(spaxels) / C_KMS)
        width = self.typical_width.val * jnp.exp(self.log_width(spaxels))
        σ = jnp.sqrt(width**2 + self.lsf.val[spaxels.idx] ** 2)
        line = jnp.exp(self.log_flux(spaxels)) / (σ * jnp.sqrt(2 * jnp.pi))
        return line * jnp.exp(-0.5 * ((λ - centre) / σ) ** 2) + self.continuum(spaxels)

The fields work in the same units as the positions, so length scales are in arcseconds. A Domain describes the region the spaxels cover, and each field chooses its Fourier modes for the length scales its prior allows (see Geometry and discretisation):

# sketch
from spectracles import Domain

spaxels = data.sky_data
domain = Domain.from_points(spaxels.x, spaxels.y)
n_spaxels = data.flux.shape[1]


def field(variance_prior):
    kernel = Matern32(
        length_scale=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(60.0, 20.0)),  # arcsec
        variance=Parameter(prior=variance_prior),
    )
    return FourierGP(kernel, domain=domain)


model = build_model(
    Halpha,
    log_flux=field(LogNormal(1.0, 0.5)),
    velocity=field(LogNormal(100.0, 50.0)),  # (km/s)²
    log_width=field(LogNormal(0.1, 0.05)),
    typical_width=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(0.3, 0.2)),  # Å
    lsf=Known(jnp.median(data.lsf_σ, axis=0)),
    continuum=PerSpaxel(n_spaxels, Parameter(dims=n_spaxels, prior=Normal(0.0, 0.05))),
)

docs.title: The posterior
docs.text:
The forward model evaluates the model at every wavelength, which gives an array with the same (wavelengths, spaxels) shape as data.flux. Pass data.mask to the likelihood so that bad pixels are skipped:

# sketch
from spectracles.inference import GaussianLikelihood, LatentSpace, Posterior


def forward(m):
    return jax.vmap(m, in_axes=(0, None))(data.λ, spaxels)


posterior = Posterior(
    LatentSpace(model),
    forward,
    GaussianLikelihood(data.flux, data.i_var, mask=data.mask),
)

From here, fitting and results are the same as for any other model: see Priors and inference.

docs.title: Maps on the sky
docs.text:
Fields can be evaluated anywhere in the domain, so a map can be drawn on a regular grid rather than at the fibres. domain.grid makes one over the whole domain, and data.sky_to_radec turns its offsets back into RA and Dec for the axes:

# sketch
grid = domain.grid((200, 200))
gx, gy = grid.x.reshape(200, 200), grid.y.reshape(200, 200)
ra, dec = data.sky_to_radec(gx, gy)

flux = posterior.map_samples(lambda m: jnp.exp(m.log_flux(grid)), samples)
flux_map = flux.mean().reshape(200, 200)

Areas far from any fibre are only constrained by the prior, so mask or grey them out when you show the map.

docs.title: Other things in the data
docs.text:
• data.v_bary: the barycentric velocity correction for each spaxel, in km/s.
  • data.mjd: the time of each exposure.
  • data.tile_idx, data.ifu_idx, data.fibre_idx: which tile, IFU and fibre each spaxel comes from, also in data.sky_data.
  • data.with_sky_origin(ra, dec): the same data with offsets measured from a centre of your choice, e.g. to put several datasets on one frame.

docs.title: Building models
docs.text:
A spectracles model is an ordinary Equinox module. You write a class that holds spectracles components (fields, per-spaxel terms, parameters) and say in __call__ how they combine into a prediction. build_model then turns it into a model you can inspect, change and fit.

This page builds a small two-line model step by step. To fit it, see Priors and inference.

import equinox as eqx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
from jax import random

from spectracles import (
    Domain,
    FourierGP,
    Known,
    Matern32,
    Parameter,
    PerSpaxel,
    SpatialDataGeneric,
    build_model,
)
from spectracles.priors import LogNormal, Normal

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

docs.title: Where the data are
docs.text:
A model is evaluated at a set of points on the sky. SpatialDataGeneric holds their positions x and y, and an index idx for each point (usually which spaxel it is). Here the positions are offsets from the centre of the field, in arcseconds:

N_SPAXELS = 400
xy = random.uniform(random.PRNGKey(0), (2, N_SPAXELS), minval=-600.0, maxval=600.0)
spaxels = SpatialDataGeneric(x=xy[0], y=xy[1], idx=jnp.arange(N_SPAXELS))

The positions can be anywhere: they don't need to lie on a grid. Use whatever units suit your data; length scales are then in the same units.

A Domain describes the region the data cover. Fields use it to work in your units:

domain = Domain.from_points(spaxels.x, spaxels.y)

For LVM data, SpatialDataLVM also carries the tile, IFU and fibre of each point. lvm_tools builds it for you from the DRP output: its FitData.αδ_data is a SpatialDataLVM. See LVM data. If your models need something else per point (an exposure number, say), subclass SpatialData and add it:

from equinox import field

from spectracles import SpatialData
from spectracles.model.data import convert_to_flat_array


class ExposureData(SpatialData):
    x: jax.Array = field(converter=convert_to_flat_array)
    y: jax.Array = field(converter=convert_to_flat_array)
    idx: jax.Array = field(converter=convert_to_flat_array)
    exposure: jax.Array = field(converter=convert_to_flat_array)

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
A field is a quantity defined continuously across the sky, such as a line flux or a velocity. FourierGP is a Gaussian-process field. It needs a kernel, which sets how smooth the field is, and the domain:

field = FourierGP(
    Matern32(
        length_scale=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(40.0, 12.0)),  # arcsec
        variance=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(1.0, 0.5)),
    ),
    domain=domain,
)
print(field.n_modes, field.padding)

The field is represented by Fourier modes on a box larger than the domain. The number of modes and the size of the margin are chosen for you, so that the field is accurate (to 0.1%) for every length scale its prior allows. Geometry and discretisation explains the choice, how to change it, and how to check a fit afterwards.

The kernels are Matern12, Matern32, Matern52 and SquaredExponential, from roughest to smoothest. Each takes a length_scale and a variance.

A field can be evaluated at any points inside the domain, not just where the data are. That is how you make a dense map after fitting.

docs.title: Means and positive fields
docs.text:
A field can have a mean, and a link that transforms it. A line flux, for example, is positive, and often best modelled as the exponential of a GP:

flux = FourierGP(
    Matern32(
        length_scale=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(40.0, 12.0)),
        variance=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(1.0, 0.5)),
    ),
    domain=domain,
    mean=Parameter(prior=Normal(0.0, 1.0)),
    link="exp",
)

This field is exp(GP + mean). link="softplus" (with lower=) is another positive option, which grows linearly rather than exponentially. The mean is a parameter like any other, fitted with its own prior.

docs.title: Per-spaxel terms
docs.text:
Some quantities don't vary continuously across the sky, such as a calibration offset for each spaxel. PerSpaxel has one value per spaxel, looked up by idx:

per_spaxel = PerSpaxel(N_SPAXELS, Parameter(dims=N_SPAXELS, prior=Normal(0.0, 0.01)))

For LVM data there are also PerIFU, PerTile and PerIFUAndTile in spectracles.model.spatial.

docs.title: Your model
docs.text:
Now write the model itself. Here, two emission lines share one velocity field, and each has its own flux field. The rest wavelengths are Known: constants that are never fitted.

C_KMS = 299_792.458


class Line(eqx.Module):
    rest_wavelength: Known
    flux: FourierGP
    velocity: FourierGP
    width: Parameter

    def __call__(self, wavelength, data):
        centre = self.rest_wavelength.val * (1 + self.velocity(data) / C_KMS)
        flux = self.flux(data)
        σ = self.width.val
        return flux / (σ * jnp.sqrt(2 * jnp.pi)) * jnp.exp(-0.5 * ((wavelength - centre) / σ) ** 2)


class TwoLines(eqx.Module):
    halpha: Line
    nii: Line
    offset: PerSpaxel

    def __call__(self, wavelength, data):
        return self.halpha(wavelength, data) + self.nii(wavelength, data) + self.offset(data)

A parameter's value is .val. Any JAX code can go in __call__.

docs.title: Building it, and sharing
docs.text:
build_model takes the class and its components. To share something between components, pass the same object to both.

First make the components. There is one velocity field, velocity, and a function that makes a new flux field each time it is called:

velocity = FourierGP(
    Matern32(
        length_scale=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(40.0, 12.0)),
        variance=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(400.0, 200.0)),  # (km/s)²
    ),
    domain=domain,
)


def flux_field():
    kernel = Matern32(
        length_scale=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(40.0, 12.0)),
        variance=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(1.0, 0.5)),
    )
    return FourierGP(kernel, domain=domain, mean=Parameter(prior=Normal(0.0, 1.0)), link="exp")

Then build the model. The same velocity object goes to both lines, so the model has one velocity field, not two. Each line gets its own flux field:

halpha = Line(
    rest_wavelength=Known(6562.8),
    flux=flux_field(),
    velocity=velocity,  # shared
    width=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(1.0, 0.2)),
)
nii = Line(
    rest_wavelength=Known(6583.5),
    flux=flux_field(),
    velocity=velocity,  # shared
    width=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(1.0, 0.2)),
)
offset = PerSpaxel(N_SPAXELS, Parameter(dims=N_SPAXELS, prior=Normal(0.0, 0.01)))

model = build_model(TwoLines, halpha=halpha, nii=nii, offset=offset)

A shared parameter is fitted once, with one prior. Two separate parameters that happen to have the same prior, like the two widths here, are fitted independently.

docs.title: Fields built from other fields
docs.text:
Two common constructions have their own classes. FieldFromRatio writes one field as another times a ratio, which is useful when the ratio is the quantity of interest. The ratio is modelled through its base-10 log, and the mean of that field is the typical log ratio:

from spectracles import FieldFromRatio, FieldPlusScatter

log10_ratio = FourierGP(
    Matern32(
        length_scale=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(60.0, 20.0)),
        variance=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(0.1, 0.05)),
    ),
    domain=domain,
    mean=Parameter(prior=Normal(-0.5, 0.3)),
)
nii_flux = FieldFromRatio(base=halpha.flux, log10_ratio=log10_ratio)  # Hα flux × ratio

FieldPlusScatter(field, scatter) adds a separate value for each spaxel to a field, for a quantity with some spaxel-to-spaxel scatter that a continuous field can't follow:

scattered = FieldPlusScatter(
    field=flux_field(),
    scatter=PerSpaxel(N_SPAXELS, Parameter(dims=N_SPAXELS, prior=Normal(0.0, 0.05))),
)

For anything else, such as the sum of two fields, write the arithmetic in your model's __call__.

docs.title: Looking at the model
docs.text:
get_parameter_summary lists every parameter by its path, with its shape, prior and whether it is free. A shared parameter appears at every location it is used, with "Shared from" naming the one place it is stored:

model.get_parameter_summary()

print_model_tree(show_sharing=True) prints the structure, and plot_model_graph() draws it, with an arrow from each component to what it uses:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(18, 8))
model.plot_model_graph(ax=ax, show=False)
fig.savefig("model_graph.png")

Both lines point to the same velocity node: it is one field.

docs.title: Evaluating
docs.text:
Call the model with a wavelength and the data. To get a spectrum at every spaxel, map over wavelengths with jax.vmap:

wavelengths = jnp.linspace(6550.0, 6600.0, 200)
spectra = jax.vmap(model, in_axes=(0, None))(wavelengths, spaxels)
print(spectra.shape)  # (wavelengths, spaxels)

(200, 400)

To call a single part of the model, such as the velocity field on a dense grid, use for_evaluation() first. It gives a copy in which shared values are filled in everywhere:

grid = domain.grid((100, 100))  # 100 × 100 points over the whole domain
velocity_map = model.for_evaluation().nii.velocity(grid).reshape(100, 100)

domain.grid((n, m), padding=...) can also reach past the domain, as far as a field's own padding: domain.grid((100, 100), padding=velocity.padding).

(Without for_evaluation(), model.nii.velocity would fail: the shared field lives at halpha.velocity, and nii only holds a reference to it.) Use the copy for evaluation only; keep the original for fitting.

docs.title: Setting and fixing values
docs.text:
set takes a dict from path to value (an array of the parameter's shape), and returns a new model:

model = model.set({"halpha.width": jnp.array([1.2]), "nii.width": jnp.array([1.2])})

set_fixed_status fixes or frees parameters by path. A fixed parameter keeps its value and isn't fitted:

model = model.set_fixed_status(["offset.spaxel_values"], [True])

Priors and fixing can also be set by glob pattern with with_priors, e.g. model.with_priors({"*.width": LogNormal(1.0, 0.2), "offset.*": "fixed"}). Free, fixed and Known explains the difference between the three kinds of parameter.

docs.title: Saving and loading
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

from spectracles import load_model, save_model

save_model(model, Path("two_lines"))
model = load_model(Path("two_lines"))

A saved file holds the whole model, including the code of your classes, so it only loads with the Python and package versions that wrote it. This is likely to change (see the roadmap).

docs.title: Built-in spectral components
docs.text: For simple cases you don't need to write the line yourself: Gaussian(A, λ0, σ) is a Gaussian line whose amplitude, centre and width are each a spatial model, Constant(c) is a flat continuum, and WindowConstant(c, λ_min, λ_max) is flat within a wavelength window. See the API reference.

docs.title: Current limitations
docs.text:
• Parameters must be attributes, not items in a list, tuple or dict. Putting one in a container raises an error; support is planned for 1.1.
  • MultiFourierGP (several fields evaluated together) is disabled until 1.1.
  • Fields are stationary: the kernel is the same everywhere on the sky.
  • Domains are square. An elongated footprint gets a square box.
  • Choosing modes for you needs the kernel's continuous form (spectral_density and covariance), which the built-in kernels have. For other kernels, give n_modes (and padding).

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: Planned work, roughly in order. Nothing here is covered by the stability promise until it is released.

docs.title: One way to fit
docs.text: Models can currently be fitted two ways: with OptimiserFrame and schedules (using prior_logpdf losses), or through the latent space (Posterior with NIFTy.re, BlackJAX or optax). These will be unified: optimisation will move to the latent space, schedules and VI stages will share one vocabulary, and the prior_logpdf losses will be deprecated.

docs.title: Power-law kernels with deviations
docs.text:
A kernel whose power spectrum is a power law plus smooth deviations from it, as in NIFTy's correlated-field model: the log amplitude is linear in log k, plus an integrated Wiener process in log k with a learnable flexibility (and optionally asperity), with its linear trend removed so the slope stays identifiable. It suits broadband fields that have no single correlation length. Alongside it:

  • LogLogLinear's amplitude m_0 will be defined at a pivot wavenumber on the mode grid, rather than at k = 1, so that it doesn't depend strongly on the slope;
  • modes and padding chosen automatically for kernels without a length scale;
  • the discretisation diagnostic and docs extended to these kernels.

docs.title: Parameters in lists, tuples and dicts (1.1)
docs.text:
Parameters, and modules holding them, must currently be named attributes of a module; build_model raises a clear error otherwise. 1.1 will support lists, tuples and dicts, with paths such as lines[0].flux or lines['Ha'].flux, so models with a variable number of components (e.g. emission lines) can be built in a loop. Existing paths are unchanged.

It also brings back MultiFourierGP, which holds its kernels in a list and raises NotImplementedError until then. It batches several fields through one NUFFT, since fields in one model usually share a frequency grid, to make multi-field models faster on GPU. (#4)

docs.title: Lazy draws for large fields (1.2)
docs.text: posterior.draws(samples, to="model") evaluates and holds every draw in memory. For many samples of a field on many points, summaries will be computed in chunks of samples (streaming mean and variance; quantiles in chunks of points), with the full draws built only on request.

docs.title: 1D and 3D fields
docs.text: Fields are two-dimensional: FourierGP takes positions x, y and a square Domain. Fields in one dimension (e.g. along wavelength or time) and three (e.g. position on the sky and wavelength, or a volume) will use the same Fourier representation, through jax-finufft's 1D and 3D transforms. That means a Domain and spatial data with any number of axes, kernels and the discretisation diagnostic in d dimensions (the error rates depend on d), and the automatic choice of modes and padding per axis.

docs.title: Saving fits rather than models
docs.text: save_model pickles the whole model with dill, including the code of your model classes, so a saved file is tied to the Python and package versions that wrote it. Since the model's structure comes from your own code and can be rebuilt, saving is likely to change to store only what a fit produces: the parameter values or latents (and samples), loaded back into a model you build the same way. save_model and load_model would then be deprecated.

docs.title: Corner plots from draws
docs.text: Draws.corner(...), a small wrapper around corner (an optional extra): hyperparameters only by default (exclude_fourier_coeffs=True), labels from the parameter paths, vector parameters split into columns, ringed scatter points with step histograms, and every corner keyword (including fig, to overlay several methods) passed through.

docs.title: Docs on Zensical
docs.text: The documentation is built with Material for MkDocs, which reaches end of life in May 2027. It will move to Zensical, its successor from the same team, which reads the existing mkdocs.yml. lvm_tools' docs, built the same way, will move with it.

docs.title: Schedule Builder API
docs.text: A declarative, parameter-centric API for building optimization schedules with minimal boilerplate.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
from spectracles import build_schedule, free_in, free_after, init_normal
import jax.random as jr

schedule = build_schedule(
    model,
    loss_fn,
    phases=[
        (100, 0.1),  # 100 steps, lr=0.1
        (50, 0.01),  # 50 steps, lr=0.01
    ],
    params={
        "gp.coefficients": free_in(0, 1),
        "gp.kernel.*": free_after(1),
        "line.amplitude": free_in(1) | init_normal(0, std=0.1),
    },
    key=jr.key(42),
)

schedule.run_all(x=data_x, y=data_y)

docs.title: free_in(*phases)
docs.text:
Parameter is free (optimized) only in the specified phases.

"param": free_in(0, 2, 4)  # Free in phases 0, 2, and 4

docs.title: free_after(phase)
docs.text:
Parameter is free from the specified phase onwards.

"param": free_after(1)  # Fixed in phase 0, free in phases 1, 2, 3, ...

docs.title: free_until(phase)
docs.text:
Parameter is free up to and including the specified phase.

"param": free_until(1)  # Free in phases 0 and 1, fixed afterwards

docs.title: fixed_in(*phases)
docs.text:
Parameter is fixed only in the specified phases, free elsewhere.

"param": fixed_in(0)  # Fixed in phase 0, free in all other phases

docs.title: Initialization Helpers
docs.text: Initialize parameters at the start of a phase.

docs.title: init_value(phase, value)
docs.text:
Set parameter to a specific value.

"param": free_after(1) | init_value(1, 2.5)  # Set to 2.5 at start of phase 1

docs.title: init_normal(phase, mean=0.0, std=1.0)
docs.text:
Initialize with random normal values. Requires passing key to build_schedule.

"param": free_in(0) | init_normal(0, mean=0.0, std=0.1)

docs.title: init_uniform(phase, low=0.0, high=1.0)
docs.text:
Initialize with random uniform values. Requires passing key to build_schedule.

"param": free_in(0) | init_uniform(0, low=-1.0, high=1.0)

docs.title: Combining Specs
docs.text:
Use | to combine free/fixed specs with initialization:

"param": free_in(0, 1, 2) | init_normal(0) | init_value(2, 1.0)

docs.title: Pattern Matching
docs.text:
Glob-style patterns match parameter paths:

Pattern Matches "param" Exact match "inner.param" Exact nested match "*.param" inner1.param, inner2.param, etc. "gp.kernel.*" All attributes of gp.kernel "gp.*.lengthscale" gp.kernel.lengthscale, gp.mean.lengthscale, etc. "**.lengthscale" Any lengthscale at any depth

docs.title: Phase Specification
docs.text:
Phases are tuples of (n_steps, learning_rate) or (n_steps, learning_rate, optimizer):

phases = [
    (100, 0.1),  # Uses default optimizer (adam)
    (50, 0.01),
    (50, 0.001, optax.sgd(0.001)),  # Custom optimizer
]

docs.title: Full API
docs.text:
schedule = build_schedule(
    model,  # ShareModule to optimize
    loss_fn,  # Loss function
    phases,  # List of phase specs
    params,  # Dict of pattern -> ParamSpec
    default_optimizer="adam",  # "adam" or "sgd"
    managed=False,  # Return ManagedOptimiserSchedule if True
    get_filter_spec_fn=get_opt_filter_spec,  # Selects which leaves are optimised
    Δloss_criterion=None,  # Early-stopping threshold (None = off)
    key=None,  # PRNG key for random initialization
)

docs.title: Early Stopping
docs.text:
Pass Δloss_criterion to let phases exit before their full n_steps. From step 100 onwards, every 50 steps, a phase stops if the loss changed by less than Δloss_criterion over the previous 50 steps:

schedule = sp.build_schedule(
    model,
    loss_fn,
    phases=[(5000, 0.1), (5000, 0.01)],
    params={"**": sp.free_in(0, 1)},
    Δloss_criterion=1e-2,
)

The same threshold applies to every phase. build_schedule defaults to None (no early stopping). A PhaseConfig constructed directly defaults to 1e2.

docs.title: Shared Parameters
docs.text:
When parameters are shared, only specify the parent path (not the shared copies). The builder validates this and will error if you try to specify a shared path directly.

# If 'b' is shared from 'a':
params = {

docs.text:
schedule = build_schedule(
    model,
    loss_fn,
    phases=[
        (200, 0.1),  # Phase 0: Warm up coefficients
        (100, 0.05),  # Phase 1: Refine with kernel
        (50, 0.01),  # Phase 2: Fine tune everything
    ],
    params={
        # Coefficients: always free
        "*.coefficients": free_in(0, 1, 2),
        # Kernel params: free after warm-up
        "*.kernel.*": free_after(1),
        # Amplitude: reinitialize at phase 1
        "line.amplitude": free_after(1) | init_normal(1, std=0.5),
    },
    key=jr.key(0),
)

schedule.run_all(x=x, y=y)
final_model = schedule.model_history[-1]

Log-log-linear CFM kernel: log-amplitude PSD is linear in log(k).

docs.title: spectracles.FourierGP
docs.text:
Bases: SpatialModel

A Gaussian-process field, represented by Fourier modes on a periodic box.

With a domain, coordinates and length scales are in the domain's units (e.g. arcsec), and the field lives on a periodic box of the domain plus padding × extent on each side. The modes and padding are then chosen for you, so that the field matches its kernel to tol over the range of length scales it can take (by default, its prior's 1% to 99% quantiles):

FourierGP(kernel, domain=domain)
FourierGP(kernel, domain=domain, tol=1e-4, length_scale=(30.0, 300.0))
FourierGP(kernel, domain=domain, n_modes=(301, 301), padding=0.15)  # by hand

Without a domain, coordinates must already lie in [-π, π], the length scale is in those units, and n_modes is needed.

A field can have a mean, a Parameter added to the GP, and a link that transforms the result, e.g. for a positive line flux:

FourierGP(kernel, domain=domain, mean=Parameter(prior=Normal(0.0, 1.0)), link="exp")

With a mean, the GP's own constant (k = 0) mode is dropped, so the mean alone sets the field's average over the box; the kernel's variance is still the field's pointwise variance.

docs.title: spectracles.optimise.opt_schedule.ManagedOptimiserSchedule
docs.text:
Multi-phase optimization schedule with state tracking and control.

Extends OptimiserSchedule with phase state management, allowing you to: - Run phases one at a time with run_next_phase() - Skip phases with skip_phase() - Reset and re-run with reset() or reset_from_phase() - Inspect progress with get_phase_status(), is_complete(), etc.

Phases must be run in order. The schedule tracks which phases are pending, running, completed, or skipped.

Attributes:

Name Type Description phases

List of Phase objects defining the schedule.

model_history

List of models, one for initial state plus one after each completed phase.

phase_states

List of PhaseState values tracking each phase's status.

current_phase_index

Index of the next phase to run.

initial_model

The original model (kept for reset functionality).

Examples:

>>> schedule = ManagedOptimiserSchedule(model, loss_fn, phase_configs)
>>>
>>> # Run phases one at a time
>>> schedule.run_next_phase(x=x, y=y)
>>> print(f"Phase 0 loss: {schedule.loss_history[-1]:.4f}")
>>>
>>> # Check status
>>> print(schedule.get_phase_status())
{'current_phase': 1, 'total_phases': 3, 'completed_phases': 1, ...}
>>>
>>> # Skip a phase if needed
>>> schedule.skip_phase(1)
>>>
>>> # Run remaining phases
>>> schedule.run_all(x=x, y=y)
>>>
>>> # Reset and try again
>>> schedule.reset()
>>> schedule.run_all(x=x, y=y)
See Also

OptimiserSchedule: Simpler version without state tracking. build_schedule: Declarative API with managed=True option.

docs.text:
Build an optimization schedule using a parameter-centric specification.

This function provides a declarative way to specify which parameters should be free or fixed in each phase, with automatic pattern expansion for parameter paths.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default model ShareModule

The ShareModule to optimize.

required loss_fn Callable[..., float]

Loss function to minimize.

required phases list[PhaseSpec | PhaseSpecFull]

List of phase specifications. Each is either: - (n_steps, learning_rate): Uses default optimizer - (n_steps, learning_rate, optimizer): Uses specified optimizer

required params dict[str, ParamSpec]

Dictionary mapping parameter patterns to ParamSpecs. Patterns support glob-style matching: - "*" matches any single component - "**" matches any number of components

required default_optimizer Literal['sgd', 'adam']

Default optimizer type ("sgd" or "adam").

'adam' managed bool

If True, return a ManagedOptimiserSchedule with state tracking.

False get_filter_spec_fn Callable[[ShareModule], Callable]

Function to get filter spec for optimization.

get_opt_filter_spec Δloss_criterion float | None

Early-stopping threshold applied to every phase. From step 100, every 50 steps, a phase exits early if the loss changed by less than this over the last 50 steps. None (default) disables early stopping.

None key PRNGKeyArray | None

PRNG key for random initializations. Required if any init_normal or init_uniform specs are used.

None

Returns:

Type Description OptimiserSchedule | ManagedOptimiserSchedule

An OptimiserSchedule or ManagedOptimiserSchedule ready to run.

Examples:

>>> schedule = build_schedule(
...     model, loss_fn,
...     phases=[
...         (100, 0.1),    # Phase 0: 100 steps, lr=0.1
...         (50, 0.01),    # Phase 1: 50 steps, lr=0.01
...         (50, 0.001),   # Phase 2: 50 steps, lr=0.001
...     ],
...     params={
...         "gp.coefficients": free_in(0, 1, 2),
...         "gp.kernel.*": free_after(1),
...         "line.amplitude": free_in(1, 2) | init_normal(0),
...     },
... )
>>> schedule.run_all(data)
